source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (CHI '25)
finding: Largest controlled test of LLM help with problem reframing. Using GPT-4o did not raise the novelty or the usefulness of the frames people wrote, in any of the three LLM modes, compared with working alone.
numbers: 456 crowd participants recruited, 280 kept after filters. 4 conditions (manual, direct generation, free-form chat, structured by Dorst's reframing theory), 3 design problems, Latin-square assignment. 15 expert designers rated 36 frames each for novelty and usefulness. Power analysis: n=280 gives 95% power for a medium effect. All between-condition tests p > 0.05.
quote: using LLMs does not help improve the quality of problem frames
limits: Only GPT-4o. Crowd participants, 3 problems, about 23 minutes per task. Instruction was to submit the 2 best frames, which may favour filtering over breadth. Other frame qualities (evocative, persuasive) not tested. Reported as null, not proof of no effect.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for SCHEMA O8 being [S]: a plain LLM reframe slot is not shown to help. Do not make reframing a default step. Gate it on a failed check (G1) and select among frames by code, not by the model.

source: Shin et al. (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing, expert vs novice analysis
finding: With LLM help, designers who understood reframing well made more novel frames than novices. The LLM widened the skill gap instead of closing it. Novices felt less agency.
numbers: Experts = 3 or more correct on a reframing quiz. In LLM conditions experts' frames were 12.54% more novel than novices' (t = 2.70, p = 0.01). Largest gap in free-form chat, 20.84% (t = 2.31, p = 0.06, not significant). No usefulness gap (all p > 0.05). Perceived helpfulness (CSI) 64.28 direct, 64.85 structured, 61.01 free-form (SD 17 to 20), no difference between modes.
limits: Expertise measured by a short quiz. The gap is correlational. Structured Dorst flow did not raise perceived helpfulness (H3 rejected). Of 218 LLM users, 93 reported trouble building on LLM frames: not novel (31), repetitive (14), not useful (12).
agent_relevance: The value of an LLM reframe depends on a selector that knows what a good frame is. Our program-side check (does the new frame change what a test or output says?) has to play the expert's role; the model cannot.

source: Sood, Wan, Paris, Grace (2026) What makes LLM-generated Answers Valuable for Research Problem Reframing? (ICCC 2026)
finding: Small two-session study of research students. A prompt that used Dorst's frame structure produced the most answers that students found interesting, and most students said the top answers made them rethink their question. Two answer profiles emerged: reinforcing (strengthens the current question) and reorienting (shifts it).
numbers: 7 research students, 3 questions each, 27 answers each (3 per strategy per question, 3 strategies), 189 answers per strategy in total. Interesting: Dorst-frame 29/189, direct 17/189, all-content 17/189. Among top-3 answers: Dorst-frame 11 (52%), direct 7 (33%), all-content 3 (14%). 5 of 7 students said the top-3 answers made them rethink their question to some extent.
quote: LLMs have already been shown to fail at supporting problem reframing in design contexts
limits: N=7, self-selected students, subjective ratings, no outcome measure. Individual preferences varied. Authors say the Dorst prompt used jargon some students disliked.
agent_relevance: Weak positive signal that a structured frame prompt beats a bare 'reframe this' prompt (about 1.7x the interest rate), against the null in c01. Worth one ablation arm in open mode: Dorst-style 'approach it as if ...' slot vs plain restatement.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers? (NAACL)
finding: On 1,600+ everyday problems that need unusual tool use, GPT-4 mostly fails to notice when a problem has no solution. It proposes infeasible actions. Humans notice more often but have higher variance.
numbers: Dataset: 78% solvable, 22% unsolvable (1,306 solvable and 377 unsolvable rated by humans). GPT-4 alone: 18.9% efficient solution, 37.5% infeasible solution on solvable items. Majority-of-humans 79.3% correct vs GPT-4 73.3%. Best of 4 human answers near perfect. Llama2-7b falsely calls solvable items unsolvable; GPT-4 almost never says unsolvable (very low in category C).
limits: Human annotation of correctness. Everyday physical problems, not open-ended research. Scale alone (Llama2 7b/13b/70b) did not unlock creativity.
agent_relevance: Problem finding includes noticing a problem is unsolvable or ill-posed. GPT-4-class models do not do this by default. A 'declare unsolvable / ask for missing info' option must be an explicit slot with its own check.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver, prompting scaffolds
finding: Two scaffolds helped GPT-4 a little: step-wise self-reflection cut infeasible answers, divergent-then-convergent prompting raised efficient answers. Smaller models did not gain from self-reflection.
numbers: 180 sampled solvable problems, zero-shot. Self-reflect: infeasible solutions down 9.7% (vs 4.3% for div-conv). Div-conv: efficient solutions up 6.5% (vs 2.2% for self-reflect). Div-conv helped GPT-4, Claude2 and Llama2-13b; self-reflect did not help Claude2 or Llama2-13b.
limits: Points as reported in the paper's text; single run on one 180-item sample; GPT-4 as judge of gains done by human annotation. Gains are single-digit.
agent_relevance: Matches G1/G2: reflection helps only where a concrete check (is the step feasible?) exists. Divergent-then-convergent maps to our open mode with a code-side selector.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks? (NeurIPS 2025 D&B)
finding: Models can often solve a fully specified problem but cannot reliably pick the one missing fact to ask about. They do well when the problem is simple math and badly on logic and planning.
numbers: 4 sets: Logic-Q, Planning-Q, GSM-Q, GSME-Q; 1-sufficient constraint problems, multiple-choice 'which question to ask'. Models: GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Gemma 2. Over 80% on GSM-Q and GSME-Q; under 50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q. Chain of thought and few-shot examples gave no significant gain across all models in Logic-Q or Planning-Q.
limits: Multiple choice (the model need not invent the question). Exactly one missing variable. Models of early 2025; the paper shows a Gemini 2.5 Pro trace only qualitatively.
agent_relevance: Choosing what to ask is a separate skill from solving. It should be a slot with a program-side check (e.g. does the answer determine the target variable?), not left to the model's judgement.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench, ablations
finding: Solving ability is necessary but not enough for asking well. Models also fail to say 'not sure' when information is missing.
numbers: Restricting to items where the model solved at least one well-specified variant: Planning-Q accuracy rose slightly, Logic-Q unchanged, neither reached 100%. In GSM-Q and GSME-Q, question accuracy shifted from +39% to about -10% depending on the model. 'Not sure' detection: in Planning-Q all models were at most 5% better than a random baseline; Gemini Thinking, Claude 3.5 and GPT-4o said 'not sure' on only 1.4%, 4.6%, 0.7% of cases where the true rate was 41.8%.
limits: Zero-shot setting for the 'not sure' numbers. Planning-Q problems are hard, so low detection may reflect difficulty.
agent_relevance: Supports G10/G12-style rule: do not trust the model's own sense of 'enough information'. Detect underspecification by code (a solver that cannot determine the target) and only then open the ask slot.

source: Fan, Li, Sun, Zhou (2025) Missing Premise exacerbates Overthinking: Are Reasoning Models losing Critical Thinking Skill?
finding: Reasoning models spend far more tokens on ill-posed questions (a needed premise removed) and rarely abstain. Non-reasoning models answer short and spot the problem faster. Longer thinking does not improve abstention.
numbers: 4 curated sets (MiP-Formula 50 unsolvable formulas, MiP-SVAMP, MiP-GSM8K, MiP-MATH). Reasoning models used 2x to 4x more tokens on missing-premise questions than on normal overthinking. Reasoning models show thinking words (alternatively, wait, check) far more than non-reasoning models, and more still on missing-premise items.
limits: Math-style ill-posedness made by deleting a premise. Models of early 2025. Abstention and suspicion judged by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G11 (think briefly) and G1: in an agent loop, an unsolvable framing makes extra thinking worse. The impasse detector should cap tokens and route to an 'ask / declare ill-posed' slot, not to more reasoning.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Missing Premise exacerbates Overthinking, in-process suspicion
finding: Reasoning models often notice early that a premise may be missing, but do not commit to it. They keep re-reading the question and guessing the user's intent.
numbers: Step-level analysis (steps split by blank lines, GPT-4o majority vote of 3): most reasoning models first suspect unsolvability in the early steps, yet abstain rarely. Only some models, for example o1, abstain at a high rate. Reasoning chains show repeated 'revisit question', 'visit knowledge', 'propose assumption', 'self doubt', 'pause/check' patterns.
limits: Exact per-model suspicion rates are in Table 4 and were not copied here; the claim is qualitative from text.
agent_relevance: Detection is cheap and early; commitment is the weak step. A program-side rule 'if suspicion text appears in the first steps, stop and run the ask-or-reframe slot' could use the model's early signal without trusting its later reasoning (G10).

source: Deng et al. (2023) Rephrase and Respond: Let Large Language Models Ask Better Questions for Themselves
finding: Having the model rewrite and expand the question before answering raised GPT-4 accuracy on many tasks, up to near 100% on the hardest-for-it tasks. Bigger gains for stronger models.
numbers: 10 tasks, subsets of 220 items (full set for Dates Understanding). GPT-4 zero-shot: Last Letter Concatenation improved to almost 100% with RaR. GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Vicuna-13b all improved on most tasks; GPT-4 gained most; GPT-3.5 and Vicuna dropped slightly on some tasks (e.g. Sports). Two-step RaR (stronger model rephrases, weaker answers) helped weaker responders. Zero-shot CoT lowered Chinese Idiom accuracy vs original question, RaR did not.
limits: Gains are largest where the original question was badly worded (ambiguous, e.g. 'even day'); on CSQA with well-formed questions the gain was marginal. Exact table values not copied. Accuracy by exact match.
agent_relevance: This is the only cheap 'restate the problem' slot with a measured gain. It is clarification of wording, not discovery of a new problem. Use as S1 input hygiene; keep it separate from O8 reframe. Rephrase is by a stronger model, answered by any.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review rated LLM-agent research ideas as more novel than expert human ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility. Differences held across three statistical tests.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition (human, AI, AI + human rerank); 79 reviewers; about 300 reviews; N=104 participants overall. Mean novelty 4.84 human, 5.64 AI, 5.81 AI reranked (p < 0.05, Welch t-test with Bonferroni correction). Overall score correlates with novelty r = 0.725 and excitement r = 0.854.
limits: NLP prompting topics only. Ideas not executed. Human ideas written in 10 days by volunteers (possibly not their best). The agent used retrieval, over-generation and LLM ranking.
agent_relevance: The topic was given to the agent, so this tests idea generation, not finding the question. Still: over-generate and rank is the pattern we use; but see c12.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?, diversity and self-evaluation
finding: Open-ended question generation saturates: most of 4,000 seed ideas per topic were duplicates. The LLM judge was a weak guide to quality.
numbers: Duplicate = cosine similarity above 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Of 4,000 seed ideas per topic, only about 200 were non-duplicate. Non-duplicate share per new batch kept falling. Inter-reviewer agreement among humans was 56.1% (balanced accuracy on top vs bottom 25%),; the paper also benchmarks LLM evaluators against this human level (comparison not copied here).
limits: Embedding similarity as a duplicate proxy. NLP research topics only. Human agreement figure is for subjective idea review.
agent_relevance: Supports 'many draws' in S3 with a hard cap: after a few hundred draws extra sampling yields near-duplicates. Dedup by embedding in code. Do not use an LLM judge to choose the best frame (G5, G8).

source: Authors not verified, listed under the Grand et al. line of work (2025/2026) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Building Rational Agents that Explore and Act Like People (ICLR 2026)
finding: Language models ask poor, redundant questions in an information-seeking game. A program-side Bayesian layer (sample hypotheses, score each candidate question by expected information gain, pick the best) lifts weak models above humans and above GPT-5.
numbers: Collaborative Battleship: 42 humans, 126 games, 931 gold-labelled questions. Captain runs 54 games (18 boards x 3 seeds). Targeting F1 LM-only to full Bayesian: Llama-4-Scout 0.367 to 0.764; GPT-4o 0.450 to 0.782; GPT-5 LM-only 0.716. Win rate of Llama-4-Scout with Bayes: 82% vs humans, 67% vs GPT-5. Expected information gain up to +0.227 bits per question (94.2% of 0.531-bit ceiling). Redundant (zero-gain) questions: Llama-4-Scout 18.5% to 0.2%; GPT-4o 14.6% to 1.2%. Cost about 1% of GPT-5. Guess Who: GPT-4o 0.617 to 0.900, Llama-4-Scout 0.300 to 0.724. Question-only Bayes added just 0.021 to 0.026 F1.
limits: Closed world with an enumerable hypothesis space and a truthful answerer. Not open problem finding. Only first 100,000 characters of the HTML were read.
agent_relevance: Best machine evidence that choosing which question to ask should be done by code that scores candidate questions, with the model only proposing them. Fits G5 and the 'program decides' principle; limited to tasks with a countable hypothesis set.

source: Grand et al. (2025/2026) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later?, answering side
finding: Models answer simple questions well but fail on context-dependent ones where humans do not. Writing code to answer helps a lot.
numbers: Spotter accuracy 52.5% (GPT-4o-mini) to 92.8% (o3 mini). Code generation +13.2 points over direct; CoT + code +14.7. GPT-4.1 75.2% to 90.9% with CoT + code. Complex questions: GPT-4o 72.8% to 60.4%; Llama-4-Scout 68.0% to 54.0%. Humans 92.8% simple, 91.9% complex; human answer accuracy 92.5% overall.
limits: Game-specific. 15 models for Spotter.
agent_relevance: When a question can be answered by running code, route it to code (G2, G5). Asking and answering are different failure points.

source: Ding et al. (2023) Fluid Transformers and Creative Analogies: Exploring LLMs' Capacity for Augmenting Cross-Domain Analogical Creativity (C&C '23)
finding: GPT-3 analogies were judged helpful for rewriting a design problem, and often changed how people stated the problem. Quality depended strongly on prompt format: one example beat zero or three.
numbers: Study 1: median helpfulness 4 of 5; in about 80% of cases the analogy led to an observable change in the problem formulation. Up to 25% of outputs judged potentially harmful (80% of those due to upsetting content). Prompt engineering over 480 analogies: potential usefulness rate zero-shot 0.68, one-shot 0.82, few-shot 0.67; duplicate rate 0.24 zero-shot, 0.12 one-shot, 0.02 few-shot; unique and useful 0.43, 0.70, 0.65.
limits: GPT-3, Prolific participants, 6 design problems, no control with human-made analogies or no analogy. Helpfulness is a rating, not a measure of better final frames. Contrasts with c01 where the effect on frame quality was null.
agent_relevance: Analogy as a reframing seed is a plausible O8 source. But the match between 'changes the formulation' (80%) and 'improves the outcome' (not shown; c01) warns us: measure the effect on the check, not on a rating.

source: Sabbah and Li (2025) When humans and large language models collaborate, problem-finding illuminates (Innovation: Organization and Management)
finding: Conceptual paper that defines problem finding as problem discovery plus problem definition, and proposes a human-LLM 'Augmented Problem-Finding' framework with research propositions. No experiment.
numbers: No measured results. Illustrated with one fictitious startup scenario (o3-mini scans customer feedback and flags 3 challenges: interface overload, insufficient personalisation, fragmented integration). Cites Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi (1976) as finding that artists who spent more time defining their problem produced more original and valued work.
limits: Propositions only. Scenario is invented. Secondhand statement of the 1976 result.
agent_relevance: Useful for vocabulary (discovery vs definition) and a map of where LLMs may help (scanning many inputs, summarising). Not evidence. Do not cite as support for any schema element.

source: Authors not recorded (2024) Tree-based problem-solution exploration with fine-tuned LLMs (arXiv 2402.06053)
finding: A system that maps problem to solution and solution back to a new problem statement, then walks a tree of neighbouring problems, as a way to refine and widen problem statements. Evidence is thin: no human evaluation.
numbers: Pythia-Chat-Base-7B with two LoRA adapters; 313 of 400 company descriptions yielded valid problem and solution pairs (303 train, 10 test). Cosine similarity of generated to reference, problem to solution: .85 (temp 0.1), .80 (temp 1.0), random .39. Solution to problem: .78, .75, random .23. Exploration: 10 problems, depth 6, k=4 neighbours, 14,000 generations.
limits: Only 10 test pairs. Training data written by gpt-3.5-turbo. Problem refinement shown only by examples. Paper has internal conflict on the temperature setting.
agent_relevance: An existing loop that does problem to solution to restated problem. Treat as a design sketch only; no evidence that it helps. Round-tripping through a solution could be tested as one O8 variant.

source: Jain and Garimella (2026) Knowing What's Missing: Assessing Information Sufficiency in Question Answering
finding: Asking the model first to list what specific information is missing, then verifying against the text, gives better sufficiency judgements than asking 'is this enough?' directly, especially on inferential questions.
numbers: Identify-then-Verify: several hypotheses about missing info, semantic consensus, then a verification pass. Gains on FaithEval over 15% after reconfiguration; explanation alignment 4.02/5 vs 3.89/5 for both baselines. Accuracy table across HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue and CouldAsk-type sets varied: for example MuSiQue-Full 59.49 vs 68.65 between two methods.
limits: Only part of the paper was read (abstract, tables). Context sufficiency in retrieval QA, not open problem finding. LLM judges in parts of the evaluation.
agent_relevance: A concrete in-loop method: 'name the gap, then verify the gap is real' before declaring a problem under-specified. Matches G2 (check from real output) and uses sampling of several hypotheses with consensus in code (G4/G5).

source: Wang (2026) FirstResearch: Auditable Question Formation for LLM Scientific Discovery Agents (arXiv 2607.05682, v2 withdrawn)
finding: Preliminary proposal for a structured 'Research Question Certificate' (assumptions, mechanism, tension, falsifiable hypothesis, minimal decisive test, failure update rule) that scored higher than prompt baselines under LLM judges. Author withdrew v2.
numbers: 10 topics, 40 baseline packages. Gemini-2.5-Flash rescore: 4.86/5 vs 4.38/5 for the strongest baseline. Judge agreement Pearson 0.865. Certificates removed: scores below 1/5. Single repeat.
limits: Only the abstract page was read this session. LLM judges, no humans, single repeat, version withdrawn. Score for a rubric that rewards the certificate's own fields, so removal of the certificate is nearly circular.
agent_relevance: Low weight. The idea of a falsifier and a minimal test attached to each proposed question is sound, but this study cannot show it helps; judged by LLMs that see the same format (G5).

source: Anon (2026) Beyond Fixed Representations: The Vocabulary and Verifier Gaps in Open-Ended AI (arXiv 2607.09560)
finding: Position paper. Today's systems search well inside a given vocabulary but rarely decide on their own when to grow it, and cannot judge a new primitive whose value shows up only after reuse. Recalls that AM's apparent fertility came partly from the encoding, and that Eurisko had parasitic self-crediting heuristics.
numbers: No experiments in the text read. Defines a generative primitive by two tests: amortized compression and feasibility extension.
limits: Only the first 100,000 characters were read. Opinion with citations, no figures. Some claims about AM are from the paper's own summary.
agent_relevance: Warns that a self-chosen question can look new only because of how it is encoded. Argues for ablation-based tests of whether a new frame makes something solvable, which matches our check-based rule (G3).

source: Lenat (1976/1977) AM; Lenat (1983) Eurisko; Ritchie (1991) What can computers discover? (Edinburgh)
finding: Older AI system for finding problems and concepts: AM proposed concepts and conjectures in number theory under interestingness heuristics. Later critique says it was hard to replicate or extend and that its apparent creativity was easy to over-read.
numbers: No numbers on the page (abstract only; 'no online copy').
limits: Only the abstract of Ritchie's paper was read. Statements about the encoding artifact and Eurisko's parasitic heuristics come from c20, not from the primary papers. Source code never published per one forum discussion (weak).
agent_relevance: Cautionary prior art: an agent that picks its own 'interesting' problems needs an outside check on interestingness, or it drifts into self-rewarding junk (G5, G8).

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Asking Questions in Battleship with Language-Informed Program Sampling
finding: Predecessor to c13: LLM proposes natural-language questions, translates them to programs, and a Monte Carlo step scores expected information gain. LLM-only baselines could not ground questions in the board; a vision model gave no improvement over text only.
numbers: Best question EIG 0.99 bits (reported via a search summary, not checked in the paper).
limits: Known only from search snippets. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same design as c13: model proposes, program scores. Cited to date the idea.

source: Si et al. (2024) vs Shin et al. (2025): reconciling positive and null LLM creativity results
finding: LLMs score high on novelty ratings when ideas are judged by outside raters (c11), but give no measured gain when helping people reframe a given problem (c01). The two tasks differ: idea generation for a stated topic vs finding the better statement of a problem. Both use human raters, so difference is not due to LLM judges.
numbers: c11: +0.80 novelty points (5.64 vs 4.84), N=49 ideas per arm. c01: no significant difference, N=280.
limits: Different tasks, raters and models (different LLM agent vs GPT-4o), so no direct comparison.
agent_relevance: Do not generalise 'LLMs are creative' to 'LLMs find better problems'. Keep problem finding as a separately measured slot in our own runs.

source: Schema position check: SCHEMA.md O8 and section 4b vs sources c01 to c23
finding: SCHEMA.md already marks O8 'Reframe the goal' as [S] with 'LLM reframing null in one large test'. That test matches c01. Nothing found here upgrades it to [E].
numbers: Evidence tally in this file: 1 large null (c01), 1 small positive for structured prompt (c03, N=7), 1 rating-only positive (c15, GPT-3), 0 replications.
limits: Our own reading of the repository file; the tally is by this agent.
agent_relevance: Keep O8 gated by G1 (only after a failed check). Add an ablation arm for Dorst-style prompt vs plain restatement, scored by the check, not by ratings.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver, human vs GPT-4 pattern
finding: Humans are all-or-nothing on creative problems (either perfect or fail), GPT-4 sits in the middle (partly wrong or inefficient). Humans struggle with domain-specific tools, GPT-4 with physical consequences. Authors link human errors to functional fixedness.
numbers: Error types for GPT-4: wrong tool usage 42.4%, not achieving the goal 17.7%, unnecessary or wrong steps 16.9%, using unavailable tools 9.5% (so 26.4% unfaithful to the constraints in total).
limits: Error percentages from the paper's figure text; some labels may be mis-parsed from the PDF.
agent_relevance: Model errors are about constraint fidelity, not fixation. A constraint-check step run in code (does the proposal use only listed tools?) catches over a quarter of the errors cheaply (G2).
